sources: Luke 11:1-13 (as he was praying in a certain place, when he ceased, one of his disciples said, “Lord, teach us to pray”; the prayer begins “Father”; the friend at midnight: “Friend, lend me three loaves, because a friend of mine is come off his journey to me, and I have not what to set before him”; “Trouble me not, the door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed”; yet because of his importunity he will rise; “Ask, and it shall be given you: seek, and you shall find: knock, and it shall be opened to you”; a father asked for a fish will not give a serpent; “how much more will your Father from heaven give the good Spirit to them that ask him?”). Douay-Rheims (Challoner).
Matthew 6:9-13 (the longer form Catholics pray: “Our Father who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name”).
Mark 14:36 (“Abba, Father,” in Gethsemane); Romans 8:15, Galatians 4:6.
Catechism of the Catholic Church 2759-2865 (the Lord’s Prayer), 2786-2793 (“Our” Father). Prayed in the Communion Rite of every Mass. Latin: Pater noster.
check: The “why” line links the prayer’s “Father” to abba, the word Jesus prays in Mark 14:36. Luke 11:2 has only Greek pater; the link to abba is a common reading, not stated in Luke. Confirm.

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? who in your life can you talk to without picking your words carefully?
options: hold onto that ease. it’s the whole point of today’s word.
keep that feeling handy. you’ll need it in a minute.
that’s okay. this story is about being let in anyway.

steps.line: One day Jesus was praying by himself. When he finished, one of his friends said, “Lord, teach us to pray.”

steps.q: He’s about to teach them a prayer. In the oldest copies of Luke, it’s shorter than the Our Father said at Mass. Which familiar line isn’t there?
o: “Give us this day our daily bread”
steps.why: Luke’s version is five short lines. “Thy will be done” and “deliver us from evil” come from Matthew’s longer one, the version the Church prays.

steps.line: He gave them a prayer that starts with a family word: “Father.” The version prayed at every Mass begins, “Our Father, who art in heaven.”

steps.q: Isaiah had already prayed, “You, Lord, are our Father.” So what stands out in how Jesus uses the word?
o: He was the first to ever call God Father
He makes it the first word, and gives it to them
He kept the word for himself alone
steps.why: Father was already in Israel’s prayers. Here it becomes the way in, handed to friends; and in Mark, Jesus prays “Abba,” the word a child says at home.

steps.line: Then he told a story. A man knocks on his friend’s door at midnight: “Lend me three loaves. A guest has come, and I have nothing to give him.”

steps.q: The friend calls back: the door’s locked, the kids are asleep. What happens?
o: He gets up and gives him the bread
The man goes home with nothing
He tells him to try another house
steps.why: He gets up, because the man won’t stop knocking. Jesus is saying: don’t be shy with God.

steps.line: Because he kept knocking, the friend got up and gave him the bread. Then Jesus told his friends: ask, seek, knock.

steps.q: In Luke’s Greek, “ask, seek, knock” are in a tense many readers hear as keep on asking. Why might Jesus put it that way?
o: God answers only after many tries
Asking is a relationship, not one request
Asking only once would seem rude
steps.why: Not to wear God down. Many readers hear it like the friend at the door: the one who keeps knocking stays close.

steps.line: “What father, if his child asks for a fish, hands him a snake? How much more will the Father in heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask!”
Today, at every Mass, the whole room prays it together before communion. Not my Father. Our Father.
steps.label: today

steps.q: After the Our Father at Mass, everyone says, “For the kingdom, the power and the glory are yours.” Where is that line from?
o: A line added later by Protestants
The prayer’s last line in Luke’s Gospel
An ancient ending, older than any split
steps.why: A form of it is in the Didache, a Christian handbook from around the year 100, and in many later copies of Matthew. Catholics say it just after the priest’s short prayer.

say: here’s what i love. the prayer jesus gave starts at home. a friend knocking at midnight, a child asking for bread: God is closer than a neighbor and kinder than any parent.
and in the version catholics pray, there’s no “i” or “me” anywhere: give us, forgive us, lead us. even alone at night, you pray it in the plural, with everyone.

steps.q: The prayer says “give us,” “forgive us,” “lead us,” and never “me.” Someone prays it alone in their room. Who are they praying with?
o: Everyone who prays it, wherever they are
steps.why: “Our” does its work twice. God isn’t a stranger, and neither is anyone else who prays it.

today.say: say just the first two words today, out loud or silently: our father. you can watch, learn, or join in. on “our,” think of one person you’d rather leave out, and let them in.
options: that’s the bravest word in the prayer. go gently.
that counts. letting them into the word is where it starts.
